title: An AI Agent Refused to Break Its Rules During Surgery - The Career Skill Behind It
content:
An AI agent was controlling a needle
above a living mouse's brain.
Then it found a problem,
and it REFUSED to fix it.
That moment is a career lesson.

Here's what happened, as reported by WIRED.
A San Francisco biotech startup called Exin Therapeutics
connected an AI agent to a custom surgical rig.
The goal was to test a gene therapy
to see if it could reduce seizures in a mouse with epilepsy.

The team gave the agent 19 treatment options in a spreadsheet.
A veterinary surgeon opened the skull first.
Then the agent chose the therapy,
the brain region,
and the injection coordinates,
and it controlled the robotic arms and the needle.

Now here's the twist.
The team first tried Claude Opus 5.5.
It refused to guide the needle into the brain.
So they switched to Claude Sonnet 5,
which agreed to proceed.

But the team had set guardrails.
A human had to approve the injection plan.
There was an emergency button to cut the rig's motors.
And the agent was NOT allowed to edit the equipment code.

Then a glitch broke the coordinate system.
The agent correctly saw that the position was wrong.
But it would not change the code,
because its instructions said not to.
The team used a separate agent to fix the code.
A procedure that typically takes about 45 minutes
took slightly more than an hour.

To be clear,
nobody knows yet if the therapy works.

So why am I telling you this?
Because the most valuable person in that room
was not the one who wrote the best prompt.
It was the person who designed the RULES.
Who approves what.
What the agent can never touch.
Where the human kill switch sits.

Here's my take.
Every company deploying agents will need people
who can design these guardrails.
Not just in labs.
In sales, in support, in finance.
Imagine a support agent that can issue refunds.
Someone has to decide the limit,
the approval step,
and what happens when something breaks.

If you want to become an AI solutions engineer,
learn this skill.
Map the workflow.
Mark every irreversible step.
Put a human on those steps.
And log everything.

That is the job that will not disappear.
It will grow.
